headline: A summit, a DNA model and plastic in the wild: what counts as proof?
teaser: Can 21 economies agree on anything big? Should we trust an AI that reads DNA before anyone checks it? And should we act on plastic before we know it harms wildlife?

articles.title: Shenzhen Hosts APEC: Can a Club of 21 Still Agree?
articles.dek: As Asia-Pacific leaders gather in Shenzhen, can a forum that needs every member's approval still deliver results that matter?
paras: Next week, the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen will become the meeting place of the Asia-Pacific. Leaders' Week of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, better known as APEC, begins on November 14, and the leaders of its 21 member economies are due to meet on November 18 and 19. It is the third time China has hosted the forum, after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. Together, APEC's members are home to roughly three billion people and produce more than 60 percent of the world's economic output, so the decisions taken in Shenzhen could, at least in theory, affect almost everyone.

APEC is an unusual organization. It was founded in 1989 to encourage trade and investment around the Pacific Rim, and its members are called "economies" rather than countries, which reflects the forum's focus on economic rather than political questions. Unlike the World Trade Organization, APEC cannot force its members to do anything. Its agreements are voluntary and must be reached by consensus, meaning that every member has to accept the final text. Supporters see this as a strength, because nobody is pushed into a commitment it cannot keep. Critics see it as a weakness, because the need for unanimous approval often reduces bold plans to cautious promises.

This year's host has chosen the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," built around three priorities: openness, innovation and cooperation. On trade, officials have been working toward a long-discussed Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, and they have set up a center to promote paperless trade. According to APEC research, replacing paper trade documents with digital ones could cut the cost of trade transactions by about 5.8 percent, a saving that would matter most to small exporters with limited staff and budgets. Such practical, technical steps rarely make headlines, yet they are where the forum has often been most effective.

Artificial intelligence is the other major item. APEC has adopted an AI Initiative for 2026 to 2030, and leaders are expected to discuss how the benefits of the technology can be shared. Here the gap between members is wide. "The benefits are very much going to those economies that are ready to embrace AI," Carlos Kuriyama of APEC's Policy Support Unit told reporters. Economies with advanced chip industries, strong digital skills and plentiful data could pull further ahead, while smaller and poorer members risk being left behind. Business leaders attending the event have called for fewer cross-border barriers, but export controls on advanced chips and strict data rules make such cooperation politically difficult.

The summit also takes place against a tense global background. APEC expects the region's economy to grow by 3.4 percent in 2026, slightly faster than last year, but it also forecasts that inflation will rise from 2.4 percent to 3.2 percent, partly because of high energy prices. US President Donald Trump has said he expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping, and possibly Russian President Vladimir Putin, in Shenzhen. Because the leaders of the world's two largest economies rarely meet face to face, many observers will pay more attention to these side meetings than to the official program.

Opinions differ on what the summit can realistically achieve. Optimists argue that APEC's size is its value: as a multilateral forum with 21 members, it gives middle-sized and smaller economies a voice and makes a simple deal between great powers less likely. They also point out that informal conversations on the sidelines can reduce misunderstandings even when no agreement is signed. Skeptics reply that the forum's declarations are often vague, and that reports suggest major trade outcomes may be saved for the Group of 20 summit instead. In their view, the meeting may turn out to be more symbolic than substantial.

Perhaps both views contain some truth. A forum that relies on consensus is unlikely to solve the hardest disputes between its most powerful members, but it can still make steady progress on less dramatic problems, such as customs paperwork or digital skills training. Whether Shenzhen is remembered as a success may therefore depend on what people expect from it: a breakthrough on the world's biggest conflicts, or a series of small, practical steps that make trade a little cheaper and cooperation a little easier.

speak.p: Some people think a group decision should be made only when everyone agrees. Others think the majority should decide so that the group can act quickly. Which approach do you prefer for making decisions in a class or club? Use specific reasons and an example.
speak.hint: State your choice → reason 1 (fairness / speed) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week, leaders of APEC's 21 member economies meet in Shenzhen. APEC only makes decisions that every member accepts, so its agreements are voluntary. Some people say this makes the forum fair and stable; others say it makes the forum too weak to solve big problems. In your opinion, are international forums that work by consensus still useful today? Why or why not? (Lena says: Yes. Consensus means that every country, including small ones, has a voice, and countries are more likely to keep promises they freely agreed to.) (Marcus says: I disagree. When every member can block a decision, the final statement becomes so vague that nothing really changes. Big problems need faster and firmer action.)
steps: Decide: consensus forums are useful, or too weak.
Give one reason, such as fairness to small members or slow decisions.
Add an example, such as a group project or a school rule.
Respond to Lena or Marcus, then conclude in one sentence.

articles.title: AlphaGenome 2: Can AI Read Our DNA One Cell at a Time?
articles.dek: Google DeepMind's new model predicts how DNA changes affect individual cell types, but should we trust results that no one outside the company has checked yet?
paras: Every cell in your body carries almost exactly the same DNA, yet a brain cell behaves very differently from a skin cell or an immune cell. The reason is that each type of cell switches different genes on and off. This creates a problem for scientists who study disease: a small change in someone's DNA, called a variant, might be harmless in most of the body but damaging in one particular type of cell. On November 11, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2, an artificial intelligence model designed to predict exactly these cell-specific effects.

The original AlphaGenome, announced in 2025, could read long stretches of DNA and estimate how a variant would change gene activity, but its predictions were averaged across whole tissues such as the liver or the lungs. The new version is what researchers call a conditional model. A user gives it a sequence of up to one million DNA letters together with a chosen condition, such as a specific cell type or cell state, and the model predicts what happens in that condition alone. It was trained on bulk and single-cell data from humans and mice, including more than 100 million individual cell profiles from 68 tissues. It can also predict DNA methylation, a chemical tag that helps control whether genes are active, which the first version could not do.

DeepMind reports impressive gains. On a test built from a single-cell map of 28 types of immune cells, AlphaGenome 2 identified 30 percent of the variants thought to cause changes in gene activity, compared with 16 percent for the earlier model and other specialized tools. In one example, the model reproduced a published discovery about inflammatory bowel disease: a distant variant that overactivates a gene called ETS2 in particular gut immune cells. Perhaps most usefully, researchers can describe a new cell state by uploading gene-activity data from just a few dozen cells, without retraining the whole model. "What makes AlphaGenome 2 exciting is how it adapts directly to new single-cell data without retraining," said Sarah Teichmann, a co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas.

Supporters believe tools like this could speed up medical research considerably. Large genetic studies have linked thousands of DNA variants to traits and illnesses, from height to type 2 diabetes, but in most cases nobody knows which variant actually matters, which gene it affects or in which cells. Testing every possibility in a laboratory would take decades and cost enormous sums. If a computer model can narrow thousands of candidates down to a short list, scientists can focus their expensive experiments on the most promising leads.

Yet there are good reasons for caution. The headline benchmark results come from DeepMind's own preprint, a paper that has not yet been peer reviewed, and no independent team has so far evaluated the new version. A separate preprint led by researchers at the Charité hospital in Berlin, posted on November 9, tested the original AlphaGenome and found that it often failed to follow certain DNA disruptions through to the rest of a gene; its authors argued that systematic testing and laboratory checks remain essential. DeepMind itself states that the model is intended for research only and is "not validated or approved for clinical or diagnostic use."

Access raises a further question. AlphaGenome 2 is free for non-commercial research through an online interface, while commercial access is available only in a private preview. Its more detailed predictions also demand more computing power than the original model. Some scientists welcome the free academic access, but others worry that an important research tool controlled by a single technology company could shape which questions get studied and who can afford to study them. Unlike open-source software, a tool offered through a company's interface can be changed, limited or withdrawn at the company's discretion.

On balance, AlphaGenome 2 looks like a genuine step forward rather than a finished solution. It is best understood as a powerful hypothesis generator, a source of educated guesses that must still be tested in real cells. If independent researchers confirm DeepMind's results, the model could help explain why the same genetic variant causes trouble in one tissue but not another. Until then, the most scientific response is the one researchers usually recommend: interested, but not yet convinced.

articles.title: Plastic in the Blood: Even Remote Wildlife Can't Escape
articles.dek: A Nature study found microplastics in wild animals far from any town, but should we act before we know whether the plastic causes harm?
paras: The Pantanal, in western Brazil, is the largest tropical wetland on Earth, a seasonal flood plain famous for its jaguars, giant otters and huge flocks of birds. If any place in South America could be described as untouched, it might be here. Yet a new study published in the journal Nature has found tiny pieces of plastic in the blood of every animal the researchers sampled in the region, including animals living more than 65 kilometers from the nearest development and more than 112 kilometers from the nearest waste facility.

Microplastics are fragments of plastic smaller than five millimeters. Some are manufactured at that size, but most form when larger items such as bags, bottles and packaging slowly break apart under sunlight, heat and friction. Because they are light and long-lasting, they travel easily. Scientists have already detected them in deep ocean trenches, on mountain peaks and in human blood, so finding them in wildlife is not in itself a surprise. What makes this study unusual is the way it connects the plastic inside an animal's body to the places where that animal actually lives and travels.

The international team, led by Dr. Marcia Ferraz of the University of British Columbia Okanagan in Canada, took blood samples from 47 free-ranging lowland tapirs and giant anteaters in three Brazilian regions: the heavily deforested southern edge of the Amazon, a farming area in the Cerrado savanna, and a relatively undisturbed ranch in the Pantanal. The animals had also been fitted with GPS collars, so the scientists knew how close each one came to roads, towns and waste sites. Microplastics were found in 43 of the 47 animals, at an average of 73.8 particles per milliliter of blood, a level within the range previously reported in humans.

The pattern was clear. Animals living in landscapes more heavily changed by people, and those that moved closer to human development and waste facilities, carried more plastic. However, distance offered only partial protection. Even where human influence was effectively zero, the team's model predicted a baseline of about 10 particles per milliliter. The researchers suggest that wind and water carry plastic fragments far beyond the places where they are thrown away. "This is the first study to link microplastics inside a wild animal's body to where that animal lives and travels," said co-author Dr. Michael Noonan.

The findings raise uncomfortable questions about waste management. Brazil's human footprint, a measure of how strongly people shape the land, grew by about 42 percent between 2001 and 2020, compared with 26 percent worldwide. In many rural and interior areas, rubbish collection and treatment have not kept pace with this growth, so plastic that is dumped or left in the open can escape into the wider environment. For conservationists, the study suggests that protecting wildlife means paying attention not only to forests and rivers, but also to rubbish bins.

Still, the authors are careful not to overstate what they found. The study measured exposure, not harm, and it shows an association rather than direct cause and effect. "We don't yet know what these particles are doing to the animals' health, and that's what worries us," Dr. Ferraz said. Laboratory studies of microplastic damage often use doses far higher than those found in nature, so their results may not apply to wild animals. Moreover, tapirs and anteaters already face habitat loss, pesticides, wildfires and climate change, which makes the effect of plastic hard to separate from other stresses.

This uncertainty divides opinion on what to do next. Some argue for the precautionary principle: since plastic is now found almost everywhere and is extremely difficult to remove, societies should cut plastic waste now rather than wait for proof of damage. Others respond that limited money for conservation should go first to threats that are already known to kill animals, such as deforestation and fire, until research shows how dangerous microplastics really are. Both sides, however, agree on one point: when even the blood of animals in a remote wetland contains plastic, the idea of truly untouched nature needs to be rethought.
